pairs.rationale: Both narrate a leper approaching Jesus and saying that Jesus can cleanse him if willing. Matthew describes bowing before Him, while Mark describes pleading and kneeling.
Both describe Jesus touching the leper, declaring His willingness and commanding cleansing, followed immediately by the disappearance of leprosy.
Both record a strict instruction not to publicize the healing, followed by showing oneself to the priest and making Moses' prescribed offering as testimony.

Both place a centurion's appeal for his servant in Capernaum. Matthew presents the centurion approaching Jesus directly; Luke narrates the appeal through Jewish elders sent by him. The modes of approach are not silently harmonized.
Both identify a centurion's seriously ill servant as the reason for the appeal. Matthew specifies paralysis and severe suffering, whereas Luke says the valued slave was ill and about to die.

Jesus' stated readiness to come in Matthew corresponds to His accompanying the elders toward the centurion's house in Luke. Luke's communication proceeds through messengers rather than Matthew's direct dialogue.

Both give the centurion's declaration that he is unworthy to have Jesus enter his roof and that a word will suffice to heal the servant. Luke delivers the declaration through friends and adds his unworthiness to approach personally.
Both use the centurion's position under authority and his commands to soldiers and a slave as the concrete analogy for the efficacy of Jesus' command.
Both narrate Jesus marveling at the centurion's faith and declaring to the following crowd that He has not found such faith even in Israel.
Both picture people arriving from distant directions to recline in God's kingdom alongside the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Luke also names north and south and includes the prophets.

Both contrast inclusion with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom with exclusion accompanied by weeping and grinding of teeth. Matthew calls the excluded sons of the kingdom and adds outer darkness; Luke addresses those cast outside.

Both conclude the centurion episode with the servant well. Matthew directly joins healing to Jesus' response to the centurion's faith and specifies that hour; Luke reports the messengers finding the slave healthy on returning home.
Both place the healing in Simon Peter's household and identify his mother-in-law as lying ill with a fever. Mark also names Andrew's house and the accompanying James and John.
Both describe Jesus taking or touching the woman's hand, the fever leaving, and her rising to serve. Matthew says she served Him, while Mark says she served them.

Both describe people bringing sick and demon-afflicted persons at evening, followed by healings and expulsions of demons. Matthew says He healed all who were ill; Mark's summary says He healed many and adds the prohibition on demons speaking.

Matthew explicitly applies Isaiah's servant passage to Jesus' healings. Its wording about taking weaknesses and carrying diseases differs from this Saints Isaiah text, which says the servant bears our sins and suffers pain for us; the connection is identified without replacing either English wording.
Both introduce the lake crossing by Jesus directing departure to the other side and leaving the crowd. Mark places the direction in the evening and describes taking Him in the boat.
Both record a prospective follower promising to follow Jesus wherever He goes. Matthew identifies the speaker as a scribe, whereas Luke leaves him unnamed and places the exchange on the road.
Both contrast the shelters of foxes and birds with the Son of Man's having nowhere to lay His head in the response to the prospective follower.
Both present a would-be follower asking first to leave and bury his father. Luke explicitly begins with Jesus' call to follow, while Matthew identifies the speaker as another disciple.
Both give the striking instruction to let the dead bury their own dead. Matthew joins it to following Jesus; Luke adds the commission to proclaim God's kingdom.
Both put Jesus and His followers in a boat at the start of the storm crossing. Mark describes leaving the crowd and other boats accompanying Him, details absent from Matthew's short boarding notice.
Both place Jesus asleep in a boat endangered by a severe storm and waves. Mark specifies His place in the stern on a cushion and says water was already filling the boat.
Both have the disciples wake Jesus because they are perishing. Matthew addresses Him as Lord and asks salvation; Mark addresses Him as Teacher and asks whether He cares.
Both connect Jesus' rebuke of wind and sea with great calm and a rebuke concerning the disciples' fear and faith. Matthew places the question before the calming; Mark places it afterward.
Both end the storm episode with the question of who Jesus is, prompted by the obedience of wind and sea. Matthew describes amazement; Mark emphasizes great fear.

Both describe meeting demon-afflicted people associated with tombs after the crossing. Matthew names the Gadarenes and two men, while Mark names the Gerasenes and focuses on one man; the place-name and participant-count differences remain explicit.

Both contain a cry asking what Jesus, identified as God's Son, has to do with the afflicted speaker and an appeal concerning torment. Matthew has plural speakers and adds before the appointed time; Mark reports one man's cry and says Son of the Most High God.
Both identify a large herd of pigs feeding near the exorcism scene. Matthew describes the herd as far from the men, while Mark places it there near the mountain.
Both record the demons asking Jesus to send them into the pigs. Mark's narration focuses on one afflicted man, unlike Matthew's two men.
Both narrate Jesus permitting the departure, the spirits entering the pigs, and the herd rushing down the bank and drowning in the sea. Mark adds an approximate herd count; Matthew gives none.
Both describe the pig herders fleeing and reporting what happened in the city. Mark also mentions the countryside; Matthew explicitly includes the report about the demon-afflicted men.

Both conclude the encounter with local people asking Jesus to leave their territory. Matthew describes the whole city coming to meet Him, whereas the cited Mark verse gives the request without that collective description.

Both introduce the paralytic-healing setting with Jesus returning to His home setting. Mark explicitly names Capernaum; Matthew calls it His own city after the lake crossing and does not name the city in this verse.

Both describe a paralytic being brought to Jesus, Jesus seeing their faith, and His declaration that the man's sins are forgiven. Mark adds four bearers and the opening in the roof; Matthew gives a shorter account.
Both describe scribes responding to Jesus' forgiveness declaration by regarding it as blasphemy. Mark further states their objection that only God can forgive sins.
Both have Jesus perceive the scribes' inward reasoning and challenge what they are thinking in their hearts. Matthew calls the thoughts evil; Mark explicitly says He perceived them in His spirit.
Both contrast the ease of saying sins are forgiven with telling the paralytic to rise and walk. Mark includes taking up the bed within the second alternative.
Both connect the healing command with demonstration that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins, then direct the paralytic to rise, take his bed and go home.
Both report the man rising and leaving after Jesus' command. Mark explicitly mentions his immediately taking the bed and leaving before everyone; Matthew simply reports his rising and going home.
Both show the witnesses responding by glorifying God. Matthew emphasizes fear and authority given to human beings; Mark emphasizes amazement and the declaration that they had never seen such a thing.

Both narrate Jesus calling a man seated at a tax station with Follow Me, and the man rising to follow. Matthew names him Matthew; Mark names him Levi son of Alphaeus. The cross-reference compares the narratives without resolving the different names.

Both describe Jesus and His disciples reclining at table among many tax collectors and sinners. The comparison concerns the shared meal setting without resolving the Matthew/Levi naming difference in the adjoining call accounts.
Both record religious critics asking the disciples why Jesus eats with tax collectors and sinners. Matthew names Pharisees; Mark specifies the scribes of the Pharisees.
Both answer the criticism with the physician analogy: the strong or healthy do not need a physician, but the sick do. Mark continues with the call of sinners within the same verse.

Jesus explicitly cites the preference for mercy rather than sacrifice. Hosea supplies that wording and continues with knowledge of God rather than whole burnt offerings; it does not itself contain Matthew's following statement about calling sinners.

Both ask why John's disciples and the Pharisees fast while Jesus' disciples do not. Matthew makes John's disciples the questioners; Mark introduces the practice and reports people putting the question.

Both use the bridegroom's presence to explain why the wedding party does not fast and predict fasting when he is taken away. Matthew's opening question speaks of mourning; Mark's speaks directly of fasting.
Both illustrate incompatible old and new with an unshrunk patch pulling away from an old garment and making the tear worse.
Both explain that new wine bursts old wineskins and destroys wine and skins, then require fresh skins for new wine. Matthew adds that both are preserved.

Both have a ruler approach Jesus and ask Him to lay hands on his daughter so she may live. Mark names Jairus and describes her as near death at this point; Matthew reports her as already just dead. The initial conditions differ rather than being silently merged.
Both narrate Jesus going with the ruler after the request concerning his daughter. Matthew mentions His disciples following too; Mark emphasizes the large crowd following and pressing Him.

Both describe a woman with twelve years of bleeding approaching behind Jesus and touching His garment. Matthew specifies its fringe; Mark adds the unsuccessful treatment history and her hearing about Jesus.
Both give the woman's own reasoning that touching Jesus' clothing will suffice for her to be saved or made well. Matthew states that she said it within herself.

Both have Jesus address the woman as daughter and say that her faith has saved her. Mark adds a dismissal in peace and freedom from the affliction; Matthew explicitly dates her recovery from that hour.
Both place Jesus at the ruler's house amid noisy mourning. Matthew specifically names flute players, while Mark describes people weeping and wailing loudly.
Both record Jesus saying the child is not dead but sleeping, followed by the mourners laughing at Him. Mark also narrates putting everyone outside within this target range.
Both have the outsiders removed, Jesus take the girl's hand, and the girl rise. Mark preserves His spoken command and her age and walking; Matthew abbreviates those details.

A later, distinct healing encounter likewise involves two blind men crying for mercy and addressing Jesus as Son of David. Matthew 9 places its approach before entering a house, whereas Matthew 20 places the men beside the road at Jericho; the events are not identified as one.

Both healing settings explicitly raise believing in Jesus' ability: Jesus asks the blind men whether they believe He can act, while in Mark He answers a father's if Thou canst and the father professes faith with a plea about unbelief. The sufferers and exchanges are different.

Both distinct blind-healing episodes describe Jesus touching the men's eyes. The later Jericho account reports compassion and immediate sight; this verse relates the outcome to faith. Shared action does not make the occasions identical.

Both distinct encounters conclude with the blind men's eyes receiving sight. The Jericho verse does not include Matthew 9's command to keep the healing unknown, and no secrecy instruction is inferred for that later event.

Both describe healed recipients publicizing their experience despite a preceding instruction not to tell. Matthew concerns the blind men spreading the report through the region; Mark concerns the cleansed leper, whose publicity limits Jesus' movements.

Both introduce an exorcism involving muteness. Luke calls the demon mute and narrates the afflicted person's speech after its departure; Matthew explicitly calls the brought man mute and demon-afflicted. The narratives' settings are not identified as one.
Both join expulsion of the demon with the formerly mute person's speaking and the crowd's amazement. Matthew adds the crowd's claim about nothing like it having appeared in Israel.
Both answer the exorcism with an accusation that Jesus acts by the ruler of the demons. Matthew identifies the accusers as Pharisees; Luke says some of them and explicitly names Beelzebul.

This same-book ministry summary repeats Jesus' teaching in synagogues, proclamation of the kingdom's good news and healing of every disease and infirmity. The earlier summary specifies Galilee, while this verse says all the cities and villages.
Both explain Jesus' compassion for crowds through the comparison with sheep lacking a shepherd. Mark proceeds to His teaching them; Matthew describes them as harassed and cast down.
Both describe the harvest as plentiful and the workers as few. Luke places the saying in the commissioning of the larger group, while Matthew addresses His disciples before the Twelve's mission.
Both direct prayer to the Lord of the harvest to send workers into His harvest. The shared saying does not erase the different mission settings.
Both have Jesus gather the Twelve and give them authority connected with demons and healing disease. Luke also states the commission to proclaim God's kingdom within the cited range.
Both apostolic lists include Simon named Peter and James and John as Zebedee's sons. Matthew includes Andrew in this verse; Mark places Andrew in the following verse, outside this cited pair.
Both lists name Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus and Thaddaeus. Matthew calls Matthew a tax collector; Mark's cited verse does not add that description.
Both apostolic lists name Simon the Cananaean and Judas Iscariot, and identify Judas as the one who handed Jesus over.

Matthew's instructions restrict this mission away from Gentile routes and Samaritan cities. Acts later explicitly commissions witness in Samaria and to the earth's end. This is a contrast between commissions in different narrative periods, not an assertion that their geographical instructions are identical.

Jesus later describes His own mission as to the lost sheep of Israel's house, the same specifically named group to which He directs the Twelve here. This is a same-book repetition in a different encounter.
Both commission the Twelve to proclaim the kingdom. Matthew supplies the message that the kingdom of the heavens has drawn near; Luke says to proclaim God's kingdom and heal.

Both mission instructions include authority over demons and healing the sick. Matthew additionally names raising the dead, cleansing lepers and giving freely; those additional commands are not supplied by this Luke passage.

Both prohibit taking money on the mission journey. Mark's allowance of a staff and its prohibition of bread and a bag belong to its fuller instruction and are not silently transferred to Matthew's different equipment list.

Both restrict mission equipment and disallow two tunics. Matthew also forbids sandals and a staff, whereas Mark permits a staff and instructs wearing sandals; this real equipment difference is retained.
Both tell the messengers to remain in the household entered until leaving the place. Matthew adds inquiry about a worthy host before the stay.

Both direct a greeting on entering a house. Luke explicitly gives the peace greeting, while Matthew's next verse explains the peace conveyed by the greeting; the mission groups differ in their narrative settings.
Both describe peace resting on a receptive household member and otherwise returning to the messenger. Matthew speaks of a worthy house, while Luke calls the recipient a son of peace.
Both direct messengers leaving a place that refuses reception or hearing to shake dust from their feet. Mark calls it testimony to them; Matthew specifies house or city.
Both warn that Sodom's treatment on the coming day will be more bearable than that of a city rejecting the messengers. Matthew also names Gomorrah and explicitly says day of judgment.
Both picture the mission as vulnerable animals sent among wolves. Matthew says sheep and adds prudence as snakes and innocence as doves; Luke says lambs without those added comparisons.
Both warn of disciples being handed to councils and beaten in synagogues. Mark places the warning in a later discourse and also names rulers and kings.
Both predict appearance before governors and kings because of Jesus, for a testimony. Matthew explicitly adds the nations among the recipients of testimony; the discourse settings differ.
Both tell those handed over not to be anxious about their defense beforehand because the needed speech will be given at that hour.
Both identify the Spirit as the source of the disciples' speech under arrest. Matthew says the Spirit of your Father speaks in you, while Mark says the Holy Spirit rather than you is speaking.
Both warn of brothers handing brothers to death, fathers handing over children and children rising against parents to have them killed.
Both predict hatred because of Jesus' name and promise salvation to the person who endures to the end. The repeated warning appears in different discourse settings.

Acts supplies a concrete later example of flight to other cities when hostility threatens the messengers: they learn of a plan involving stoning and flee to Lystra and Derbe. It illustrates flight under persecution, not Matthew's further timetable concerning the Son of Man's coming.
Both say a disciple is not above the teacher. Luke adds that a fully trained disciple will be like the teacher, while Matthew also gives the slave-master comparison.

Both use the relationship between master and subordinate to explain why disciples can expect treatment like Jesus'. John makes persecution explicit; Matthew's example is the household master's being called Beelzebul, a detail absent from the cited John verse.
Both say that covered things will be revealed and hidden things become known. Matthew uses this assurance to tell disciples not to fear their opponents.

Both contrast speech in darkness or private rooms with public hearing in the light and proclamation from housetops. Matthew commands public proclamation of His teaching; Luke predicts the public exposure of private speech.

Both distinguish people who can kill the body from the one with authority concerning Gehenna and direct fear toward the latter. Matthew explicitly mentions destruction of both soul and body; Luke does not repeat that formulation.

Both use inexpensive sparrows to illustrate God's care. Matthew prices two at one assarion and says none falls apart from the Father; Luke prices five at two assaria and says none is forgotten before God.
Both say even the hairs of the disciples' heads are numbered, as an image of God's detailed care.
Both urge freedom from fear because the hearers are more valuable than many sparrows.

Both connect acknowledging Jesus before people with a corresponding heavenly acknowledgment. Matthew promises acknowledgment before His Father; Luke describes the Son of Man's acknowledgment before God's angels.
Both warn that denying Jesus before people leads to heavenly denial. Matthew names His Father as the heavenly audience, while Luke names God's angels.
Both challenge the expectation that Jesus' coming brings uncomplicated earthly peace. Matthew uses the image of a sword; Luke explicitly says division.
Both describe divisions involving father and son, mother and daughter, and mother-in-law and daughter-in-law. Luke gives reciprocal formulations, while Matthew states the divisions in one direction.

Matthew's statement that a person's enemies will be members of the household recalls Micah's concluding statement that a man's enemies are the men in his house. Micah also lists family divisions matching the preceding Matthew verse.

Both demand allegiance to Jesus over the closest family relationships. Matthew expresses this as not loving parents or children more than Him; Luke uses the stronger language of hating family and one's own life. The wordings are not harmonized into an exact quotation.
Both make taking or carrying one's cross and coming after Jesus a requirement of discipleship. Matthew describes the person as not worthy of Him, while Luke says the person cannot be His disciple.
Both reverse the attempt to preserve one's life: losing it because of Jesus leads to gaining or saving it. Mark explicitly adds the gospel as a cause and uses save where Matthew uses find.
Both describe reception of Jesus' messenger as reception of Jesus and reception of Jesus as reception of the One who sent Him.

The Shunammite woman's hospitality to Elisha because she recognizes him as a holy man of God illustrates receiving a prophet in that capacity. These verses narrate bread and lodging; they do not themselves state Matthew's general promise of a prophet's reward.

Both promise that giving a cup of water on account of the recipient's belonging to Jesus will not lose its reward. Matthew says cold water to one of these little ones in a disciple's name; Mark speaks of giving to the disciples because they are Christ's.
Both describe John sending disciples to Jesus after hearing reports about Him. Matthew specifies John's imprisonment; Luke explicitly mentions two disciples without naming the prison in this passage.
Both preserve John's question whether Jesus is the coming One or another should be expected. Luke records both the sending instruction and the messengers' delivery of the question.
Both direct the messengers to report to John what they have seen and heard, introducing the list of healing and proclamation signs.
Both list blind people seeing, lame people walking, lepers cleansed, deaf people hearing, dead people raised and poor people receiving good news as the reply to John's question.
Both conclude the reply to John by pronouncing blessed the person who does not stumble because of Jesus.
Both describe Jesus beginning to address the crowd about John after the messengers leave and asking whether they went into the wilderness to see a reed shaken by wind.
Both reject the image of John as a softly clothed court figure. Matthew says such people are in kings' houses, while Luke describes splendid clothing and luxury in royal palaces.
Both ask whether the crowds went to see a prophet and affirm that John is more than a prophet.

Matthew's messenger preparing the way is grounded in Malachi's announced messenger. The Saints Malachi wording has the way before My face and goes on to the Lord's coming to His sanctuary, whereas Matthew addresses Thy face and Thy way; the differences remain visible.
Both compare John's greatness among those born of women with the greater standing of the least in God's kingdom. Matthew calls him John the Baptist and says kingdom of the heavens.

Both link John with a new phase of the kingdom and use language of force or pressing. Matthew says the kingdom suffers violence and violent men seize it; Luke says the kingdom is proclaimed and everyone presses into it. The comparison does not resolve these distinct expressions into one interpretation.
Both place the Law and Prophets up to John. Luke continues with the proclamation of God's kingdom from then onward, while Matthew explicitly says the Law and Prophets prophesied until John.

Matthew identifies John with the Elijah who is to come; Luke describes John's going before the Lord in Elijah's spirit and power. This connects the Elijah role without claiming John and the historical Elijah are literally the same person.
Both use the summons for the one with ears to hear. Mark places the formula after the sower parable, while Matthew places it in the discourse about John; the occasions differ.
Both compare the present generation to children sitting in a marketplace and calling to one another, introducing the complaint about unresponsive playmates.
Both give the children's complaint that flute playing produced no dancing and lament produced no mourning response. Matthew says beating the breast, while Luke says weeping.
Both report the accusation that John has a demon in response to his abstinent way of life. Luke specifies neither eating bread nor drinking wine; Matthew says neither eating nor drinking.

Both report Jesus being called a glutton, wine drinker and friend of tax collectors and sinners, then speak of wisdom's vindication. Matthew says vindicated by her works, while Luke says by all her children; the ending differs.

Luke's woe over Chorazin and Bethsaida gives the same contrast between mighty works and the repentance that would have occurred elsewhere. Matthew's verse introduces the reproach of unrepentant cities, with those names in its following verse; the discourse settings differ.
Both pronounce woe on Chorazin and Bethsaida and say Tyre and Sidon would have repented in sackcloth and ashes if they had experienced the same mighty works.
Both warn that judgment will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon than for the reproached towns.
Both address Capernaum with the contrast between supposed exaltation to heaven and descent to Hades. Luke's verse does not include Matthew's additional comparison with Sodom's survival.

Matthew repeats the warning of more bearable judgment for Sodom, here in the reproach of Capernaum and earlier in instructions about towns rejecting the mission. This is a same-book recurring judgment comparison in different settings; the earlier verse also names Gomorrah.

Both give Jesus' acknowledgment of the Father as Lord of heaven and earth for hiding these things from the wise and understanding and revealing them to infants. Luke additionally locates His joy in the Holy Spirit.
Both complete the address with Yes, Father and an appeal to what was pleasing before Him. Luke includes it in the same verse as the preceding thanksgiving.
Both declare all things handed over by the Father and the unique mutual knowledge of Father and Son, with the Son revealing the Father to those He chooses.

Both present an invitation associated with a teacher, instruction and rest. Sirach invites the uninstructed near, speaks of a yoke and reports finding much rest after little labor; Jesus invites the burdened to Himself and promises to give rest. This is a wisdom-teaching comparison, not a claim that Sirach names Jesus.

The combination of taking a yoke, receiving instruction and finding rest recalls Sirach's invitation to put the neck beneath the yoke and receive instruction, followed by much rest. Matthew centers the invitation on learning from Jesus and adds His meekness and humility.

Jesus describes His yoke as easy and burden as light, while Sirach describes little labor yielding much rest. The comparison concerns the rewarding lightness of instruction; Sirach does not repeat Matthew's statement about Jesus' own yoke.
Both narrate Jesus and His disciples passing through grainfields on the Sabbath and the disciples plucking heads of grain. Matthew explicitly mentions hunger and eating in this verse.
Both have Pharisees challenge Jesus about the disciples' doing what is not lawful on the Sabbath in the grainfield setting.
Both answer the Sabbath challenge by asking whether the critics have read what David did when he and his companions were hungry.

Samuel narrates the priest giving David holy loaves of presentation, the bread of the Presence, after discussion about the young men's purity. This supplies the bread episode Jesus recalls; these cited verses do not themselves state Matthew's full legal restriction to priests.

The law prescribes additional burnt offerings on each Sabbath, supplying the commanded temple-service background for Jesus' argument about priests working on Sabbaths without guilt. Numbers states the offering requirement; it does not itself call the service profaning the Sabbath.

Matthew claims something greater than the temple is present. John explains Jesus' temple saying as referring to the sanctuary of His body. These are distinct ways of relating Jesus to the sanctuary; John does not repeat Matthew's greater-than comparison.

Jesus' mercy-not-sacrifice quotation matches Hosea's statement of the Lord's desire for mercy rather than sacrifice. Matthew applies it to the condemnation of the guiltless in the Sabbath dispute; Hosea continues with knowledge of God over burnt offerings.
Both conclude the grainfield controversy with the Son of Man's lordship over the Sabbath.
Both move into a synagogue scene that introduces a man with a withered hand. Matthew's verse gives the entry, while Mark includes the man's presence in the same verse.

Both place Sabbath healing under hostile scrutiny aimed at finding an accusation. Matthew reports a direct question about lawfulness, while Luke describes the scribes and Pharisees watching whether Jesus would heal.

Both appeal to rescuing a vulnerable creature from a pit or well on the Sabbath as an answer to healing objections. Matthew uses a sheep and its being grasped and lifted; Luke's supplied saying uses a son or an ox, so the examples and narrative occasions differ.

Both argue the Sabbath question in terms of doing good. Matthew concludes it is lawful to do good and compares a human's value with a sheep's; Luke asks whether doing good or evil, saving life or destroying it, is lawful.

Both give Jesus' command to stretch out the hand, the man's action and its restoration. Matthew explicitly says it became healthy like the other; Mark describes Jesus' anger and grief before the command.
Both have the Pharisees go out and take counsel about destroying Jesus after the healing. Mark additionally names the Herodians as partners in the plot.

Both describe withdrawal, crowds following and healing activity. Matthew says He healed them all and links withdrawal to knowledge of the plot; Mark lists the crowds' regions and says He healed many, so scope and wording are not made identical.

Both report a stern command not to make Jesus known. Matthew addresses the healed crowd in the surrounding narrative; Mark's immediate recipients are the unclean spirits, a difference in audience retained here.

Matthew introduces the following servant passage as fulfillment of Isaiah. The cited Saints Isaiah unit supplies the chosen servant, Spirit, restrained public conduct, bruised reed and nations' hope, though its naming and some wording differ from Matthew's quotation.

Both describe God's chosen servant, divine approval, the Spirit placed upon him and judgment proclaimed to the nations. Saints Isaiah explicitly names Jacob as servant and Israel as chosen one, whereas Matthew has My Servant and My beloved; this difference and Matthew's application to Jesus remain explicit.

Both describe the servant's refusal to cry out or raise a public voice. Matthew says no quarreling and no voice heard in the streets; Isaiah says no crying or raising the voice and no voice heard outside.

Both preserve the bruised reed and smoking wick images and join the servant's gentleness to the establishment of judgment. Matthew speaks of judgment brought to victory, while Saints Isaiah says judgment in truth and judgment set upon the earth.
Matthew's promise that nations will hope in His name matches the final clause of the Saints Isaiah servant passage, retaining this Greek-based English wording.

Both link expulsion of a demon with a mute man's speaking. Matthew additionally identifies blindness and restored sight; Luke's cited account does not mention blindness, and the settings are not asserted to be identical.

Both place the designation Son of David in a blind-healing context. Here the crowds ask whether Jesus could be that figure after a healing; in the separate Jericho episode two blind men directly address Him that way. The speakers and occasions differ.
Both accuse Jesus of casting out demons by Beelzebul, the ruler of demons. Matthew identifies the speakers as Pharisees; Luke refers to some among the observers.
Both have Jesus perceive their thoughts and answer that a kingdom divided against itself is devastated. Matthew adds divided city or house not standing; Luke gives the house-collapse formulation.
Both ask how Satan's kingdom can stand if Satan is divided against himself, in answer to the accusation that Jesus expels demons through Satan's power.
Both challenge the accusation by asking through whom the hearers' own sons cast out demons and conclude that those sons will be their judges.
Both interpret Jesus' expulsions of demons as evidence that God's kingdom has come upon the hearers. Matthew says by God's Spirit; Luke says by God's finger. The distinct imagery is preserved.
Both use the image of entering a strong man's house and first binding him before plundering his belongings.
Both declare that the person not with Jesus is against Him and the person not gathering with Him scatters.

Both contrast the forgiveness available for sins and blasphemies with the exception of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. Mark states the exclusion in terms of never having forgiveness and liability for an eternal sin; Matthew's cited verse does not use that final phrase.
Both distinguish speech against the Son of Man, which can be forgiven, from blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, which will not. Matthew adds neither in this age nor in the coming one.

Both connect a tree's character with its fruit and treat fruit as the means of knowing the tree. Matthew frames a choice between making tree and fruit good or rotten; Luke gives the good-tree and rotten-tree contrasts and examples.

Both connect speech with what fills the heart and say the mouth speaks from that abundance. Matthew addresses hostile hearers as vipers and evil; Luke places the statement in a general contrast between good and evil persons.
Both describe the good person producing good from good treasure and the evil person producing evil from evil treasure. Luke explicitly names the heart as the treasure's location.

Both state personal accountability before God or at judgment. Matthew specifically includes every idle word spoken; Romans speaks more generally of each person's giving an account of himself to God and does not repeat the idle-word criterion.

Both make a person's own speech a basis of judgment. Matthew gives a general saying about justification or condemnation by words; Luke's parable has the master judge the servant from his own mouth. The parable does not repeat Matthew's whole general rule.

Both report religious opponents asking Jesus for a sign. Matthew includes scribes and Pharisees and addresses Him as Teacher; Mark names Pharisees, specifies a sign from heaven and describes their testing purpose.
Both call the sign-seeking generation evil and allow no sign except Jonah's. Matthew adds adulterous and identifies Jonah as prophet.

Jonah explicitly spends three days and three nights in the sea creature's belly, the duration and setting Jesus names as the comparison for the Son of Man in the heart of the earth. This Saints edition numbers the Jonah verse 2:1; the comparison does not independently fix a chronology of Jesus' burial.
Both say the men of Nineveh will rise in judgment and condemn this generation because they repented at Jonah's preaching, while something greater than Jonah is present.
Both invoke the queen of the south's journey to hear Solomon's wisdom as grounds for condemnation of this generation, with something greater than Solomon now present.
Both describe a departed unclean spirit passing through waterless places in search of rest and finding none. Luke includes its decision to return in the same verse.
Both have the spirit decide to return to its former house and find it swept and arranged. Matthew additionally calls the house vacant; the Luke passage does not explicitly add that adjective.

Both narrate the returning spirit bringing seven worse spirits, their inhabiting the person and a final condition worse than the first. Matthew additionally applies the picture to the evil generation.
Both place Jesus' mother and brothers outside seeking access to Him while He is teaching. Mark says they send and call Him; Matthew says they seek to speak with Him.

Both report someone informing Jesus that His family is outside seeking Him. Matthew names mother and brothers; Mark also names His sisters. The family terms remain distinct rather than being harmonized.
Both give Jesus' answering question about who His mother and brothers are.
Both identify those present with Jesus as His mother and brothers. Matthew describes His stretching out a hand toward His disciples; Mark describes His looking around at those seated around Him.
Both define Jesus' brother, sister and mother through doing God's will. Matthew explicitly says the will of His Father in the heavens; Mark says God's will.

deferred.reason: The mountain-descent and crowd-following transition was read. No sufficiently specific independently supported counterpart to this transition was retained; generic crowd notices were not used to create a completed pair.

The report of the girl-healing spreading throughout the region was read. The parallel Mark ending describes astonishment and restricted disclosure, not the same report-spreading notice; no precise counterpart was retained in this batch.

The transition from directing the Twelve to Jesus teaching and proclaiming in their cities was read. General ministry summaries were considered but no sufficiently close counterpart to this specific transition was retained.

review_notes: Read all 194 source verse units in Matthew 8–12 from the exact pinned Saints-Translation English record. No source wording changes are proposed.
Every retained target is read in the exact pinned Saints source snapshot. Target IDs, complete ranges and ordered adjacency are verified before this review is finalized.

Real differences are stated rather than harmonized: centurion messengers versus direct approach; two Gadarene demoniacs versus one Gerasene man; Matthew versus Levi; the daughter dead versus dying at the initial approach; and mission equipment differences.

Saints Greek-based numbering and wording are retained, including Isaiah 53:4 bearing sins versus Matthew carrying diseases, Isaiah 42 naming Jacob and Israel, 1 Samuel 21:5–7 for the holy loaves, Jonah 2:1, and Sirach wisdom/yoke passages.

Same-book and same-chapter links are identified as internal comparisons rather than independent historical corroboration. Different Gospel occasions are not assumed identical merely because wording or actions overlap.
AI-assisted English passage comparison; this initial curated review is not an exhaustive concordance or an independent specialist critical-text review.
